name: Less-is-better effect
statement: An option can be valued more highly than an option that contains everything it has and more, when each is judged on its own.
meaning: The claim is about how an option is shown, not about what is in it. Judge two options side by side and the bigger one usually wins. Judge them one at a time, with different people seeing different options, and the ranking can flip. Christopher Hsee called the second arrangement separate evaluation and the first joint evaluation. His proposed mechanism is the evaluability hypothesis: some attributes carry meaning on their own and some do not. A shopper alone with a dinnerware set cannot say whether 40 pieces is generous, because nothing fixes the scale. That same shopper can see at once that some of the cups are broken. So the attribute that is easy to read drives the separate judgement even when it matters less, and the attribute that needs a comparison drives the joint judgement. The effect is a claim about evaluation mode. It is not a claim that people prefer smaller quantities.

origin.note: Three of Hsee's scenarios are the ones usually retold. Study 1 put a $45 scarf from a $5 to $50 range against a $55 coat from a $50 to $500 range, and the scarf giver was judged more generous. Study 2 priced 7 oz of ice cream overflowing a 5 oz cup above 8 oz filling a 10 oz cup. Study 4 priced a 24-piece dinnerware set above a 40-piece set holding the same three kinds of intact pieces plus 8 cups and 8 saucers, nine of which were broken. The 2023 replication team left out Hsee's Study 3 as close in design to Study 2. No copy of the 1998 paper was obtained for this entry, and every figure below from the 1998 studies is read off later papers that reprint it. Hsee had set out the evaluability hypothesis two years earlier in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, where 116 students priced second-hand music dictionaries.

evidence: The 1996 dictionary study is the cleanest statement of the mechanism, and it is weaker than the retellings suggest. Hsee gave students Dictionary A, 10,000 entries and like new, or Dictionary B, 20,000 entries with a torn cover, or both. Judged together, B drew the higher price (t = 7.11, p < .001). Judged apart, A drew the higher price, but that half of the pattern did not reach significance (t = 1.69, p = .1). The reversal itself was significant (t = 4.56, p < .001). The 1998 gift study, as Many Labs 2 reports it, put 83 people in one of two conditions and found the scarf giver rated more generous than the coat giver, 5.63 against 5.00, t(82) = 3.13, p = 0.002, d = 0.69, 95% CI [0.24, 1.13]. The dinnerware study, as the 2023 replication reports it, ran 104 people and split both ways at once: judged separately the 40-piece set drew $23.25 against $32.69 for the 24-piece set (t = 3.91, p < .001), and judged jointly the same 40-piece set drew $32.03 against $29.70 (t = 2.15, p = .039). The 2023 team's supplement says Hsee printed neither the condition sizes nor the degrees of freedom for that study, so it assumed an even split across the three conditions and derived the rest. The effect sizes it attributes to Hsee's Study 4 rest on that assumption, and this page does not carry them.

replication.headline: The separate-evaluation half of the effect is among the better-replicated findings in judgement research. Many Labs 2 ran the gift scenario on 7,646 people and got d = 0.78, 95% CI [0.74, 0.83], slightly larger than the original.
replication.detail: Many Labs 2 put Study 1 in its Slate 2 protocol, which 61 of the project's 125 samples ran, adjusting the prices for inflation and converting them where dollars would be unfamiliar. Scarf recipients rated the giver at 5.50 (SD 0.89) against 4.61 (SD 1.34) for coat recipients, t(6,569.67) = 34.20, p = 4.5e-236. Vonasch and six co-authors then ran all three scenarios in 2023 on 403 MTurk workers, 400 of whom were analysed after three refused to take part, with each person kept in the same condition throughout. Separate evaluation gave a signal every time: gift d = 0.99 [0.72, 1.25], ice cream d = 0.32 [0.07, 0.56], dinnerware d = 0.76 [0.50, 1.02], the last two smaller than the originals and the first larger. Joint evaluation, which the theory needs, held up less well. Ice cream produced the predicted more-is-better result, dz = 0.60 [0.42, 0.79]. Dinnerware gave $31.67 for the larger set against $30.35 for the smaller, dz = 0.11 [-0.06, 0.28], which the paper calls no signal, though 59% of the same people were willing to pay more for the larger set on a binomial test, p = .047. The paper's Table 5 marks four of the five effects as signals and says the means ran in the predicted direction in both joint tests. Its abstract prints different joint figures from its own results section, dz = 0.33 [.23, .43] for ice cream and dz = 0.09 [-0.05, 0.23] for dinnerware, and the abstract Crossref holds for the published article carries the same pair. This page quotes the results section and the table. Two accounts of the original gift study differ in the second decimal: Many Labs 2 prints d = 0.69 [0.24, 1.13] and the 2023 team prints d = 0.70 [0.24, 1.15]. Both are recalculations by replicators rather than figures from the 1998 paper.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: The boundary the theory predicts is joint evaluation, and it mostly holds. Put both options in front of one person and the ranking usually rights itself, which is why the effect says more about how choices are laid out than about what people want. Three cracks are worth knowing. First, the correction is not reliable: in the 2023 dinnerware replication the larger set failed to win the willingness-to-pay test in joint evaluation, and the same people rated it less attractive than the smaller set (dz = 0.38 [.21, .56]) and felt worse about its price (dz = 0.40 [.22, .57]), which the authors report as against their prediction. Second, the ice cream result turns on data cleaning. With Hsee's own rule, which drops willingness to pay above $10.39, d = 0.32 [0.07, 0.56]; with the two outliers left in, d = 0.06 [-0.18, 0.30]. Third, paying real money does not remove it. John List ran the design at a sportscard show with 241 people, 130 non-dealers and 111 dealers, bidding in a random nth-price auction. Non-dealers bid $4.86 for 10 graded 1982 Topps cards and $3.06 for the same 10 plus three cards graded poor, a gap of about 37% significant at p < 0.05 (t = 2.03, z = 2.47), and the order reversed to $3.72 against $4.52 when the bundles sat side by side (p < 0.01). Dealers bid $3.20 against $2.70, a gap of more than 15% that missed significance (z = 0.84 and t = 0.84), and List reads his dealer panel as showing the same pattern rather than escaping it. The mechanism is contested. Sher and McKenzie model the reversal as rational inference from the sample of options a person is shown, which on their account defuses the apparent breach of dominance without making the reversal irrational. Age cuts against the standard account too. Parrish and Sandgren recruited 122 children at a Charleston children's museum, kept 118 aged 3 to 9, and analysed 116 after two failed the pre-trial check. Given joint-evaluation choices between a smaller intact set and a larger damaged one, children picked the smaller set on all six trial types, all ps < .001, and on 73.85% of trials collapsed. The bias rose with age, r(103) = .284, p = .003, 95% CI [.097, .451]. No meta-analysis of the less-is-better effect was located on 21 September 2026, in Crossref bibliographic searches and web searches for the effect name, for joint versus separate evaluation and for the evaluability hypothesis.
misreadings: The dinnerware set is described wrongly in the literature that studies it. Parrish and Sandgren's abstract calls the larger set a 24-piece set with 16 additional broken dishes. The stimulus table reprinted in the 2023 replication lists 8 cups of which 2 are broken and 8 saucers of which 7 are broken, so 9 of the 16 extras are damaged and 7 are fine. Sher and McKenzie describe the same stimulus the same way, 40 pieces of which nine were broken, giving 31 intact. List's 2002 summary of the same study gets the joint-evaluation direction backwards, reporting that the smaller set wins when the two are juxtaposed, which is the opposite of the $32.03 against $29.70 the replication prints for the original. Second, the effect is not a rule that people want less. It needs an attribute nobody can size up alone and a second attribute anyone can, and it needs the two options kept apart. Sales pages, comparison tables and shelves put options together, which is the arrangement in which the effect goes away or reverses. Third, evidence that a real seller loses money by adding a cheap item is thin. List's auction is the closest thing to a market test and it used bundles built for the experiment, with the effect weakest among the professionals. The nearest marketing finding, Weaver, Garcia and Schwarz's presenter's paradox, runs over seven studies on a different mechanism, weighted averaging in impression formation, and reaches the same practical advice by another route. In their first study evaluators would pay $242.19 (SD $108.41) for an iPod Touch and cover and $176.71 (SD $86.16) for the same package plus a free music download, F(1, 40) = 4.7, p < .05, while 11 of 12 presenters chose to add the download. Fourth, joint evaluation is a boundary condition rather than a cure. It failed to restore more-is-better for dinnerware in the 2023 replication, and children show the effect under joint evaluation, more strongly the older they are.
